classification.difficultyReason: Construct reflections in both orders, including across a diagonal line, then compare final positions to determine whether reversing the order changes the result.

inlines.text: Use the first diagram for parts a–d (source part a, steps i–iv). In part e, repeat those steps for the second diagram (source part b).

children.label: a
children.prompt: First diagram — original part a(i): Copy the first diagram below.

spec.description: Eight-by-eight unit grid with perpendicular double-arrow reflection lines m and n through its centre. The marked triangle prevents use of a blank-grid template. Ordinary reflection lines and grid use house black; the original triangle retains semantic blue.
spec.mathematics: Relative to the unlabelled intersection, triangle vertices are (-3,0), (-1,3), (0,0); m is horizontal and n is vertical. Coordinates are reconstruction data and are not printed.
spec.answerVisibility: Original triangle and reflection lines only; no reflected images.

answer.short: Copy the grid, both reflection lines and the triangle as shown.
answer.worked: Draw an $8\times8$ square grid. Draw $m$ horizontally and $n$ vertically through the centre, with arrowheads at both ends. Copy the triangle with its base on $m$, its right vertex at the intersection and its top vertex one square left and three squares above the intersection.

spec.description: Complete copy of the first supplied diagram.
spec.mathematics: Original triangle and perpendicular reflection axes reproduced on an eight-by-eight unit grid.

children.label: b
children.prompt: First diagram — original part a(ii): Reflect the triangle in $m$, then reflect the image in $n$.

spec.description: Eight-by-eight unit grid with perpendicular double-arrow reflection lines m and n through its centre. The marked triangle prevents use of a blank-grid template. Ordinary reflection lines and grid use house black; the original triangle retains semantic blue.
spec.mathematics: Relative to the unlabelled intersection, triangle vertices are (-3,0), (-1,3), (0,0); m is horizontal and n is vertical. Coordinates are reconstruction data and are not printed.
spec.answerVisibility: Original triangle and reflection lines only; no reflected images.

answer.short: The final triangle is below $m$ and to the right of $n$.
answer.worked: Reflect each vertex across $m$, keeping its perpendicular distance from $m$ unchanged, and join the reflected vertices. The intermediate triangle is below $m$ and left of $n$. Reflect this image across $n$. The final triangle has one vertex at the intersection, another three squares right of it and the third one square right and three squares down.

spec.description: Blue original, dashed red intermediate image and green final image.
spec.mathematics: Reflection in m gives (-3,0),(-1,-3),(0,0); subsequent reflection in n gives (3,0),(1,-3),(0,0).
spec.answerVisibility: Complete solution figure; answer edition only.

children.label: c
children.prompt: First diagram — original part a(iii): Now reflect the original triangle in $n$, then reflect the image in $m$.

spec.description: Eight-by-eight unit grid with perpendicular double-arrow reflection lines m and n through its centre. The marked triangle prevents use of a blank-grid template. Ordinary reflection lines and grid use house black; the original triangle retains semantic blue.
spec.mathematics: Relative to the unlabelled intersection, triangle vertices are (-3,0), (-1,3), (0,0); m is horizontal and n is vertical. Coordinates are reconstruction data and are not printed.
spec.answerVisibility: Original triangle and reflection lines only; no reflected images.

answer.short: The final triangle is again below $m$ and to the right of $n$.
answer.worked: Reflect each original vertex across $n$, keeping equal perpendicular distances on opposite sides of $n$, and join the images. The intermediate triangle is above $m$ and right of $n$. Reflect it across $m$. The final vertices are at the intersection, three squares right of it, and one square right and three squares down.

spec.description: Blue original, dashed red intermediate image and green final image.
spec.mathematics: Reflection in n gives (3,0),(1,3),(0,0); subsequent reflection in m gives (3,0),(1,-3),(0,0).
spec.answerVisibility: Complete solution figure; answer edition only.

children.label: d
children.prompt: First diagram — original part a(iv): Are your answers to parts b and c the same?

spec.description: Eight-by-eight unit grid with perpendicular double-arrow reflection lines m and n through its centre. The marked triangle prevents use of a blank-grid template. Ordinary reflection lines and grid use house black; the original triangle retains semantic blue.

answer.worked: Yes. The two final triangles coincide. In either order, these two perpendicular reflections have the effect of a $180^\circ$ rotation about the intersection.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Second diagram — original part b: Repeat the steps in parts a–d (original steps i–iv) for the second diagram.

spec.description: Eight-by-eight unit grid with horizontal double-arrow line m and diagonal double-arrow line n. The diagonal rises at 45 degrees, with endpoints three squares either side of the centre. Marked geometry prevents use of the blank-grid template. Ordinary axes use house black; original triangle retains semantic blue.
spec.mathematics: Relative to the intersection, triangle vertices are (-3,0),(-1,3),(0,0); m is y=0 and n is y=x. These equations and coordinates are not printed.
spec.answerVisibility: Original triangle and reflection lines only.

answer.short: No. Reflecting in $m$ then $n$ gives the lower-left final triangle; reflecting in $n$ then $m$ gives the upper-right final triangle.
answer.worked:
i. Copy the second grid, reflection lines and original triangle.

ii. Reflect the original vertices across $m$, placing them at equal perpendicular distances on its other side. The intermediate vertices are three squares left of the intersection, one square left and three squares down, and the intersection itself. Reflect this image across $n$. The final vertices are three squares down, three squares left and one square down, and the intersection.

iii. Start again with the original triangle. Reflection in $n$ gives vertices three squares down, three squares right and one square down, and the intersection. Reflect these across $m$. The final vertices are three squares up, three squares right and one square up, and the intersection.

iv. No. The final triangles occupy different positions. The first order gives a $90^\circ$ anticlockwise rotation about the intersection; the reverse order gives a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation.

spec.description: First order: blue original, dashed red reflection in m, green final reflection in n. The original figure also supplies the copy requested in step i.
spec.answerVisibility: Complete solution figure; answer edition only.

spec.description: Reverse order: blue original, dashed red reflection in n and green final reflection in m.
